page4_img_2.png.title: Log-log scatter: Messages sent vs. Out-degree (distinct respondents)
page4_img_2.png.description: A log–log scatterplot (n = 1,063) showing each individual’s number of messages sent (x-axis, ~1 to >3,000) versus their out-degree (y-axis, number of distinct people who replied, ~1 to >300). Axes use logarithmic ticks (1, 3.1, 10, 31, 100, 316, …) and the points form a tight upward trend across several orders of magnitude. The plot (constructed only from people who received at least one reply) visually confirms the very high Spearman rank correlation (~0.97) reported in the paper: as message count increases, the number of distinct respondents grows monotonically.

page6_img_2.png.title: Developers show much higher centrality than non-developers in the email network
page6_img_2.png.description: A 3×4 table comparing mean network measures for developers (n=73) and non-developers (n=1,123) shows developers have substantially larger betweenness and normalized in- and out-degrees. Means: betweenness 0.0114 vs 0.000140, out-degree 0.00666 vs 0.000451, in-degree 0.00794 vs 0.000367 — roughly two orders of magnitude higher for developers. Two-sample t-tests give t-values of 5.07, 8.14 and 7.54 respectively, each with p < 0.001, indicating the differences are statistically significant. (Betweenness is computed as described in the paper; in/out-degrees were normalized by network size.)

page6_img_1.png.title: Spearman correlation matrix: changes vs. social-network measures (n=73)
page6_img_1.png.description: A symmetric 6×6 Spearman rank-correlation table relating total changes, source changes (srcChanges), document changes (docChanges), out-degree, in-degree, and betweenness for the 73 committers. Diagonal entries are 1; notable high correlations include changes↔docChanges = 0.932, srcChanges↔betweenness = 0.757, outdegree↔indegree = 0.971, outdegree↔betweenness = 0.955, and indegree↔betweenness = 0.917, while docChanges shows much weaker ties to the network measures (e.g., docChanges↔outdegree = 0.308). Rightmost columns report descriptive stats: means [min, max] — total changes mean=912 [0,16289], srcChanges mean=420 [0,5741], docChanges mean=492 [0,13420], outdegree mean=0.0080 [0,0.0396], indegree mean=0.0067 [0,0.0260], betweenness mean=0.0011 [0,0.0965]. These values support the paper’s claim that source-change activity is strongly associated with higher social-network status, while document changes are less so.

page5_img_1.png.title: Pruned Apache email social network showing strong reply ties (>=150 messages)
page5_img_1.png.description: Directed network diagram pruned to show only links with at least 150 reply messages: each oval is a mailing-list participant and each arrow points from sender to a respondent (i.e., the respondent replied ≥150 times to the sender). The figure reveals a dense upper cluster of core developers (e.g., ben laurie, alexei kosut, dean gaudet, brian behlendorf, jim jagielski, rob hartill, randy terbush, marc slemko) with many mutual arrows, and a separate hub around ryan bloom connecting to william a. rowe_jr., bill stoddard, jeff trawick and greg stein. These heavily linked nodes match the paper’s observation that a small set of highly connected individuals (Gaudet, Laurie, Bloom, Jagielski, Rowe) dominate conversation and act as brokers in the Apache developer email community.

page4_img_1.png.title: Log‑log distributions of messages and network degrees in Apache mailing list
page4_img_1.png.description: Four side‑by‑side log–log scatterplots (left to right) show how many participants exhibit a given count of: messages sent, replies received, social-network out‑degree, and social-network in‑degree; the vertical axis is “Number of Participants” and each horizontal axis is logarithmic (ticks ≈1, 3.1, 10, …, 3162). All four panels display a clear downward linear trend on the log–log scale (an approximate power‑law / long‑tailed distribution): most people have very low counts (one or a few messages or links) while a small number have very large counts. The out‑degree and in‑degree plots mirror this pattern, supporting the paper’s interpretation that the email social network is scale‑free / small‑world, with a few highly connected (high‑status or highly engaged) actors accounting for much of the activity.
